stem:
A 27-year-old woman with a clearly documented diagnosis of borderline personality disorder sees you as her general practitioner under a Mental Health Treatment Plan. Over the past year she has had four brief emergency presentations after superficial cutting following relationship arguments, and she describes chronic emptiness and rapid swings between idealising and devaluing her ex-partner and her sister.

She has completed adequate trials of sertraline and then escitalopram over 14 months with no lasting benefit. Her K-10 today is 28. She has no current major depressive episode by full DSM-5-TR criteria, no psychotic features, is not pregnant, drinks under 3 standard drinks per week, and has stopped occasional cannabis. She asks what treatment specifically targets the pattern of self-harm and relationship instability rather than just her mood.

data_table.Examination: Multiple healed and recent superficial linear scars to bilateral forearms. MSE reactive affect, no perceptual disturbance, no current suicidal intent.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 28. FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management for the core disorder?

options.text: Commence low-dose quetiapine 100 mg nocte for chronic affective instability
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no first-line role in the core disorder and carry metabolic risk; they may be considered short-term for acute crisis only. Would only be appropriate if a comorbid indication were present (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Commence lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg daily for affective mood swings
options.rationale: Mood stabilisers do not have robust evidence for the core disorder and the NHMRC guideline recommends against routine pharmacotherapy. Would only be considered if bipolar disorder were confirmed as a comorbidity (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Refer to a structured group-based dialectical behaviour therapy programme
options.rationale: Structured evidence-based psychotherapy is first-line for the core disorder; DBT has the strongest Australian evidence for reducing self-harm and emergency presentations and is the most widely funded modality in public services (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Trial a third SSRI at maximum dose over 12 weeks with regular monitoring
options.rationale: Two adequate SSRI trials have failed and SSRIs do not treat the core disorder; further trials are reserved for a clearly comorbid depressive episode (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Arrange voluntary inpatient admission for six weeks of behavioural work
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient admission tends to reinforce maladaptive coping and is discouraged; brief crisis admissions are used only when safety cannot be managed in the community (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

explanation.summary: The NHMRC 2013 CPG names DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy as first-line evidence-based treatments for borderline personality disorder. Medications are for comorbidities only.
key_points: First-line is structured evidence-based psychotherapy, not medication
DBT has the strongest local availability and evidence in Australia
Antipsychotics and mood stabilisers should not be prescribed for the core disorder
Prolonged inpatient admission is discouraged; brief crisis admissions only
Longitudinal data show over 80 percent achieve remission within 10 years
explanation.pearls: In context, when a patient with borderline personality disorder asks what will change the pattern itself, the answer is structured psychotherapy, not a medication substitution.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is in an established DBT programme in her 4th month. She presents to your general practice for a routine review requesting a script for regular diazepam 5 mg three times daily, saying it is the only thing that stops her cutting when she is very distressed. She has a prior history of two mixed diazepam and alcohol overdoses in her early twenties and a documented previous alprazolam dependence that took 9 months to taper. She has no current comorbid anxiety disorder meeting DSM-5-TR criteria and no current major depressive episode.

She has a written DBT crisis plan she can produce on her phone and lists her DBT therapist and after-hours mental health line as contacts. She tells you that other doctors have prescribed short PRN diazepam courses in the past and that it always helped her in the moment.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, tearful when discussing recent partner conflict, no acute intoxication, no fresh injuries.
data_table.Investigations: Nil today. Prior CBC, EUC, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg PRN twice daily for two weeks then review at the practice
options.rationale: PRN benzodiazepine use in this disorder still confers dependence and overdose risk and undermines the extinction learning DBT depends upon. Would only be considered for a short-lived non-personality crisis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch to oxazepam 15 mg three times daily as a lower-abuse-potential alternative
options.rationale: The class objection to benzodiazepines in this disorder is disinhibition and dependence rather than pharmacokinetics; oxazepam still carries these risks. Would only be preferred in a hepatic-impairment inpatient sedation scenario (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence low-dose quetiapine 25 mg nocte as ongoing symptomatic anxiolysis nightly
options.rationale: Antipsychotic use for the core disorder is not supported and adds metabolic risk without addressing the underlying skills gap. Would only be considered short-term in a documented crisis (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Commence pregabalin 75 mg twice daily as a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic option
options.rationale: Pregabalin has an established misuse and dependence profile in this population and no evidence base for the core disorder. Would only be considered for concurrent neuropathic pain (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Decline regular benzodiazepines and reinforce use of the existing DBT crisis plan
options.rationale: Regular benzodiazepines are contraindicated in this disorder given disinhibition, overdose potential, dependence risk, and interference with new learning central to DBT. The NHMRC guideline advises against benzodiazepines and prefers reinforcement of psychological crisis skills (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

explanation.summary: Regular and PRN benzodiazepines are not recommended in borderline personality disorder due to disinhibition, overdose potential and dependence, and because they interfere with the new-learning process that DBT relies on.
key_points: Benzodiazepine disinhibition can worsen self-harm and aggression
Overdose potential is high in a population with recurrent overdose behaviour
New skill acquisition in DBT is impaired by regular sedatives
Prior alprazolam dependence increases likelihood of recurrence
Reinforcing the crisis plan is the correct clinical move
explanation.pearls: In context, requests for benzodiazepines from a patient in active DBT are best met with skills coaching, not scripts.

stem:
A 24-year-old university student is referred by her general practitioner with a query of bipolar II disorder after her family raised the question. She describes rapid mood shifts every few hours which she can date to specific interactions with her partner and mother, chronic emptiness since her mid-teens, three low-lethality overdoses in the past 18 months following relationship arguments, and superficial cutting since age 14.

On detailed enquiry she has never had a period of persistently elevated or irritable mood lasting four consecutive days with a change in functioning. She has never had a sustained decreased need for sleep independent of her distress, and her energy tracks her interpersonal situation. Family history is negative for bipolar disorder; her father had recurrent depressive episodes. She has not used stimulants and her thyroid function and urine drug screen are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, no pressured speech, no flight of ideas, no grandiosity elicited today. Multiple healed and recent linear forearm scars.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative. K-10 30. Mood chart over the last month shows swings occurring within a single day and mapping onto interpersonal events.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly supports borderline personality disorder over bipolar II disorder?

options.text: Recurrent low-lethality self-harm and overdose behaviour since her mid-adolescence years
options.rationale: Self-harm is more common in the borderline construct but occurs in mood disorders too and is not the discriminator with bipolar II specifically. Would not distinguish the two on its own (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).

options.text: Mood shifts lasting hours and clearly tied to interpersonal events on a prospective chart
options.rationale: Bipolar II hypomania requires a distinct episode of at least 4 consecutive days of persistently elevated or irritable mood with functional change and is not tightly triggered by moment-to-moment interpersonal events; interpersonal-event-linked mood shifts within a day are core to the borderline construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: A negative family history for bipolar disorder in her first-degree biological relatives
options.rationale: A negative family history lowers pre-test probability but does not itself distinguish the two conditions and cannot rule out bipolar II. Would only be supportive alongside phenomenology (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

options.text: Chronic subjective feelings of emptiness across the past several years of her life
options.rationale: Emptiness features in the borderline construct but is also common in chronic depression and does not discriminate against bipolar II. Would not distinguish the two on its own (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Onset of the pattern of instability in mid-teens rather than in early adulthood
options.rationale: Both diagnoses can begin in adolescence; onset age is not a reliable discriminator between them. Would not distinguish the two on its own (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

explanation.summary: Bipolar II hypomania requires a discrete episode of at least 4 days with sustained mood elevation or irritability and a change in functioning independent of interpersonal triggers. Borderline mood shifts are typically hour-to-hour and tightly coupled to interpersonal events.
key_points: Duration criterion for hypomania is 4 consecutive days
Bipolar mood episodes are not phasically driven by interpersonal events
A mood chart tracking triggers is the most useful outpatient tool
The two disorders commonly co-occur; correct differentiation still matters for treatment
First-degree family history for bipolar shifts pre-test probability but is not diagnostic
explanation.pearls: In context, hour-scale mood shifts mapped to interpersonal events on a prospective chart is the single most useful outpatient discriminator between these two diagnoses.

stem:
A 28-year-old man is seen in your community mental health clinic after release from a 4-month custodial sentence for aggravated assault. He describes a pattern from age 12 of animal cruelty, truancy, fire-setting and property theft. He has been dismissed from four jobs for stealing, has three prior convictions for assault, and reports no remorse for hospitalising a stranger in his most recent offence, describing the man as an idiot who deserved it. He denies any past self-harm, denies chronic emptiness, and denies fear of abandonment. His relationships have been brief and instrumental; he says he ends them when the woman becomes boring.

He is not currently depressed, drinks 6 standard drinks nightly, uses methamphetamine 2 to 3 times per month, and is not psychotic today. He describes his aggression as goal-directed and premeditated when he feels disrespected, rather than as a distressed response to relationship crises.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, callous affect, no evidence of acute intoxication.
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for amphetamines. FBC, EUC, LFTs within normal limits.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours antisocial rather than borderline personality disorder?

options.text: History of three separate convictions for assault leading to a recent custodial sentence
options.rationale: Forensic history increases probability but is not diagnostic on its own; people with the borderline construct can also have violence convictions. Would only be supportive alongside the pattern of premeditation and remorselessness (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).

options.text: Comorbid daily heavy alcohol use and intermittent methamphetamine use twice per month
options.rationale: Substance use disorders are common in both diagnoses and do not discriminate between them. Would only be relevant to treatment sequencing (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic).

options.text: Premeditated instrumental aggression with absent remorse plus a childhood conduct pattern
options.rationale: Antisocial personality disorder requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 plus adult disregard for others; premeditated instrumental aggression with callous absence of remorse is characteristic and differs from the affectively driven reactive aggression seen in the borderline construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Brief unstable relationships that he ends when the partner becomes uninteresting to him
options.rationale: Relationship instability is common to both; the qualitative pattern differs but the presence of brief relationships alone is not sufficient. Would only support the diagnosis when the reason for ending is instrumental rather than fear of abandonment (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Absence of prior mental health service contact or documented psychiatric diagnosis in file
options.rationale: Many people with either diagnosis have never engaged services; service contact history is not a discriminator between the two constructs. Would only reflect access patterns (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).

explanation.summary: The core differentiating features are the developmental conduct disorder history, the premeditated instrumental quality of aggression, and the callous absence of remorse. Borderline aggression is reactive, affectively driven, and typically accompanied by guilt.
key_points: Antisocial personality requires childhood conduct disorder features before age 15
Aggression is instrumental and premeditated rather than reactive
Remorse is characteristically absent
Substance use and relationship instability occur in both and do not discriminate
Comorbid antisocial and borderline features can coexist and require both to be addressed
explanation.pearls: In context, ask about pre-15 conduct-disorder features and the quality of aggression - instrumental with absent remorse points to antisocial, reactive with subsequent guilt points to borderline.

stem:
A 29-year-old man is referred by his general practitioner because his family are concerned that he might have schizophrenia. He describes a longstanding conviction since his late teens that he can sense the intentions of people three floors up in his apartment block, and he interprets flickers in the lights as messages meant specifically for him. He has magical thinking about numbers and superstitions that he has held consistently for a decade. He has very few friends, is anxious in social settings, and speaks in a slightly odd tangential manner.

He has no clear fixed false belief held with conviction against contrary evidence, no true auditory hallucinations, no clear thought disorder on formal examination, and no functional decline over the past decade - he has held the same warehouse job for 9 years. He is not depressed, uses no substances, and has never had a discrete psychotic episode.

data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly guarded, tangential speech but redirectable. No clear delusions or hallucinations. Affect constricted. No cognitive impairment on brief testing.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis for this presentation?

options.text: Schizophrenia with predominantly negative and disorganised symptoms
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 2 or more active-phase symptoms (with at least one of delusions, hallucinations, or disorganised speech) for a significant portion of one month, plus 6 months of overall disturbance with functional decline; neither is present here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Delusional disorder of the referential subtype
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires one or more fixed delusions held with conviction against evidence for at least one month; his beliefs fall short of that threshold and are more magical than frankly delusional (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizotypal personality disorder with ego-syntonic magical beliefs
options.rationale: Longstanding odd beliefs, magical thinking, ideas of reference falling short of frank delusion, mild perceptual distortions, odd speech, and interpersonal deficits without functional decline or a discrete psychotic episode over a decade characterise this construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizoid personality disorder with preferred long-term solitude
options.rationale: Schizoid presentation is characterised by pervasive detachment and a genuine preference for solitude without odd beliefs or perceptual distortions; the odd cognitive-perceptual features here place him outside that construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Attenuated psychosis syndrome under the DSM-5 conditions
options.rationale: Attenuated psychosis syndrome describes recent-onset subthreshold psychotic symptoms typically over the past year with progression; his features have been stable for a decade with no functional decline (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Schizotypal personality disorder is characterised by pervasive cognitive and perceptual distortions, magical thinking and ideas of reference short of fixed delusion, odd speech and interpersonal deficits, present from early adulthood without a distinct psychotic episode or functional decline.
key_points: The threshold for delusion is fixed conviction held against contrary evidence
Odd speech in the schizotypal construct is tangential rather than formally disorganised
Long stable course without functional decline is against schizophrenia
Duration of subthreshold symptoms distinguishes this from attenuated psychosis syndrome
Schizoid presentation lacks the odd cognitive-perceptual features
explanation.pearls: In context, decade-long odd beliefs that stop short of fixed delusion, with preserved function, place the patient in the schizotypal construct rather than in the schizophrenia spectrum.

subtopic_detail: Avoidant PD vs social anxiety disorder
stem:
A 34-year-old man presents to your general practice reporting that he has never had a romantic partner and has no close friends outside his brother. He tells you he desperately wants closeness but has always felt inferior, socially inept, and unappealing, and he avoids new work opportunities because he expects to be criticised or rejected. His avoidance is not limited to performance or scrutiny situations - he also avoids one-to-one meetings, small dinners, and neighbourly conversations that would not involve any observable performance. He describes the pattern as present since childhood and stable.

He does not have physiological anxiety spikes when he is not in feared situations. He is not currently depressed, does not use alcohol to cope, and has held a back-office data role for 8 years. His self-view of being fundamentally inadequate persists even when he receives clearly positive feedback at work.

data_table.Examination: Alert, guarded, poor eye contact, self-deprecating speech content. No thought disorder. Affect constricted.
data_table.Investigations: Nil today. TSH within normal limits at last review.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis in this case?

options.text: Social anxiety disorder of the generalised performance subtype
options.rationale: Social anxiety typically clusters around performance and scrutiny with situational anxiety symptoms; the enduring self-view of inadequacy and avoidance of non-scrutiny interpersonal contact points beyond this diagnosis. Would be considered when the picture is limited to fear of scrutiny (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder with prominent interpersonal features
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years with vegetative features; this presentation is dominated by longstanding interpersonal avoidance and self-view rather than pervasive low mood. Would be considered if mood features dominated (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizoid personality disorder with detached interpersonal preference
options.rationale: The schizoid construct includes genuine preference for solitude and indifference to relationships; this patient wants closeness and is hurt by its absence. Would be considered when detachment is not distressing (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Avoidant personality disorder of the pervasive interpersonal type
options.rationale: Pervasive since-childhood pattern of feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to negative evaluation, and avoidance extending beyond performance situations into all interpersonal contact, with an enduring self-view of inferiority, characterises this construct rather than social anxiety disorder (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder recognised for the first time in adulthood
options.rationale: Autism spectrum diagnosis requires early-childhood social communication deficits and restricted repetitive behaviours; the description here is centred on avoidance driven by feared negative evaluation rather than communication difference. Would be considered if reciprocal-communication difficulty and restricted interests were present (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Avoidant personality disorder features an enduring self-view of inadequacy and avoidance of interpersonal contact that extends beyond performance and scrutiny situations. Social anxiety disorder is more circumscribed to feared evaluative contexts and does not require the pervasive negative self-view.
key_points: Enduring negative self-view is characteristic of the avoidant construct
Social anxiety centres on evaluative and performance situations
The schizoid construct includes genuine preference for solitude
Persistent depressive disorder requires vegetative mood features
Autism spectrum diagnosis requires early social communication difference plus restricted repetitive patterns
explanation.pearls: In context, when the wish for closeness is preserved but the self-view of inadequacy pervades every interpersonal setting, the picture goes beyond social anxiety into the avoidant construct.

stem:
A 41-year-old lawyer is referred by his general practitioner with 6 months of low mood after being passed over for promotion. He is chronically preoccupied with a sense that his talents are not recognised, that his colleagues are inferior yet somehow being favoured, and that he deserves special treatment because of his exceptional intellect. He is exquisitely sensitive to any perceived slight and describes recurrent hypochondriacal worries about his health that have prompted three specialist referrals in the past year.

Unlike an overtly grandiose presentation he is not boastful in the room, appears shy and self-effacing, and complains at length of shame and inadequacy. His relationships are marked by intense envy of successful peers, subtle contempt for those he sees as beneath him, and an inability to sustain the initial idealisation he shows new therapists once they fail to provide the mirroring he expects.

data_table.Examination: Alert, quietly spoken, shy manner, easily wounded by any exploration of his professional setbacks, subtle contempt expressed toward colleagues.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 24. TSH within normal limits. Nil other relevant investigations.

lead_in: Which construct best captures this presentation on further formulation?

options.text: Grandiose subtype of narcissistic personality disorder with overt entitlement in room
options.rationale: The overt grandiose subtype is characterised by boastfulness, exhibitionism, and open entitlement in the room; his presenting shy manner and prominent shame move the picture toward the vulnerable subtype. Would be preferred when the presenting posture is openly boastful (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Major depressive disorder with atypical features and interpersonal rejection sensitivity
options.rationale: Atypical features require mood reactivity, leaden paralysis, increased sleep or appetite, and interpersonal rejection sensitivity dominating the picture; his mood features are secondary to entrenched personality dynamics rather than an episodic mood disorder. Would be preferred if the reactive mood syndrome were primary (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Illness anxiety disorder driven by preoccupation with health across multiple domains
options.rationale: Illness anxiety is diagnosed when preoccupation with having a serious illness is the primary and enduring focus; here the hypochondriacal worries sit within a wider personality picture of grandiosity and shame. Would be preferred if illness preoccupation dominated in isolation (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Vulnerable subtype of narcissistic personality disorder with covert grandiosity and shame
options.rationale: The vulnerable presentation combines covert grandiosity with hypersensitivity to criticism, shame, envy, hypochondriasis, and quiet contempt for others behind a shy self-effacing exterior; it is often missed when clinicians expect only the overt grandiose type (Source: DSM-5-TR alternative model).

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder with sustained low mood over the past several years
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires chronic depressed mood for at least 2 years with vegetative features; the presentation is dominated by entrenched personality dynamics rather than sustained low mood. Would be preferred if chronic depressive vegetative features predominated (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: The vulnerable subtype of the narcissistic construct is easily missed because it lacks overt grandiosity in the room. Recognising the covert grandiosity, envy, shame, and quiet contempt guides engagement strategy and therapy fit.
key_points: Grandiose subtype is overt and boastful
Vulnerable subtype is shy and shame-driven with covert grandiosity and envy
Both are highly sensitive to perceived slights
Recognition affects therapy engagement rather than requiring pharmacotherapy
Mood syndromes commonly overlie the personality picture and can mask it
explanation.pearls: In context, a shy shame-driven presentation with quiet contempt and envy is often the vulnerable narcissistic construct rather than depression alone.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar covering a mixed medical ward. A 25-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted with cellulitis. Over 48 hours the nursing team has become polarised: two nurses describe her as manipulative, demanding, and undeserving of a bed, while one senior nurse and a junior doctor describe her as vulnerable, misunderstood, and mistreated by their colleagues. She has told the sympathetic staff that the other nurses are cruel, and told the critical staff that the sympathetic ones are the only ones who really care.

The medical team ask you to see her because they are worried she is escalating and want your advice about how to manage the ward-level disagreement, not just the patient. She is medically stable, not currently suicidal, and is engaged with her outpatient DBT programme. There is no acute risk needing immediate transfer.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, minimises her distress with the critical nurses and amplifies it with the sympathetic staff. No psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: Nil relevant to the request. Cellulitis parameters improving on IV antibiotics.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intervention for the ward-level dynamic?

options.text: Move her to a single room and restrict her contact to only the sympathetic nurses on each shift
options.rationale: Restricting care to the idealised subgroup entrenches the splitting rather than resolving it and burdens a small group. Would only be considered if there were a specific safety-of-staff concern (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

options.text: Commence a short course of low-dose olanzapine 5 mg nocte to reduce her interpersonal reactivity
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy does not address the team dynamic and antipsychotics have no first-line role in the core disorder. Would only be considered short-term in a documented crisis (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Discharge her home once medically fit and refer for outpatient behavioural therapy follow up
options.rationale: She is already in a DBT programme and premature discharge without addressing the ward dynamic will lead to repetition on the next admission. Would only be considered when medically fit AND the team dynamic is contained (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

options.text: Convene a brief team meeting to name the splitting dynamic and agree a consistent unified response
options.rationale: Naming the splitting dynamic in a structured team meeting and agreeing on a unified consistent approach reduces the polarisation, models containment, and is the first-line management for this specific ward dynamic (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

options.text: Ask her outpatient DBT therapist to attend the ward and provide crisis skills coaching each day
options.rationale: Outpatient DBT therapists do not routinely deliver inpatient skills coaching and this does not address the polarised staff response. Would only be appropriate as an adjunct once the team dynamic is contained (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

explanation.summary: Splitting is diagnostic data about how a patient organises relationships under stress and is best addressed at the team level. Naming it explicitly, agreeing on a unified approach, and sharing responsibility across the team is the first-line intervention.
key_points: Splitting is a systems-level phenomenon requiring a team response
Restricting care to the idealised staff entrenches the split
Medication does not address interpersonal dynamics
Consistent unified responses across the team model containment
Ward-level supervision or reflective practice reduces staff burnout
explanation.pearls: In context, when the team starts to feel split about a patient, that is diagnostic data - the intervention is at the team level, not the patient level.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is being considered for structured therapy after a year of unsuccessful supportive counselling. Her main difficulties are misreading other people's intentions, jumping to conclusions that partners and colleagues are contemptuous of her when they are not, and losing her capacity to think clearly about her own mental states when she is upset. She has had two previous suicide attempts by paracetamol overdose 3 and 5 years ago but no episodes in the past year.

She has struggled with the highly structured behavioural skills format of a previous partial DBT trial and dropped out at week 6, saying the skills felt mechanical. She is articulate, insightful when calm, and interested in understanding why she gets into these misreading spirals. She is not psychotic, is not currently misusing substances, and has stable social security housing.

data_table.Examination: Alert, thoughtful when calm, becomes anxious and prematurely certain when discussing recent interpersonal ruptures.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 26. FBC, EUC, LFT within normal limits.

lead_in: Which structured psychotherapy is the best fit for this specific presentation?

options.text: A second full trial of dialectical behaviour therapy in the same group format
options.rationale: A repeat trial of the same modality that she recently disengaged from is unlikely to succeed and other evidence-based modalities are available. Would only be considered if the reason for dropout were addressable (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Mentalisation-based therapy focused on restoring reflective capacity under arousal
options.rationale: MBT is an evidence-based structured therapy that specifically targets the loss of mentalising capacity under emotional arousal and the tendency to misread others; its reflective non-skills-based format suits patients who found DBT too mechanical (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy for depression using the standard weekly format
options.rationale: CBT for depression targets depressive cognition and behaviour and is not the first-line structured therapy for the core personality disorder. Would only be considered for a comorbid depressive episode (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

options.text: Interpersonal psychotherapy for depression focused on identified role conflicts
options.rationale: Interpersonal psychotherapy targets identified interpersonal problems in the context of a depressive episode and is not indicated as first-line therapy for the core personality disorder. Would only be considered for a comorbid depressive episode (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

options.text: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing for previously identified past trauma
options.rationale: EMDR is indicated when the presenting problem is post-traumatic stress disorder; her presentation is centred on personality-driven misreading rather than reexperiencing of trauma. Would only be considered if PTSD were prominent (Source: NHMRC PTSD Guideline).

explanation.summary: MBT is one of four NHMRC-named first-line structured therapies for borderline personality disorder. Its focus on restoring mentalising capacity under arousal is a particular fit for patients who misread others and who find the skills-based DBT format too mechanical.
key_points: MBT is a first-line NHMRC-named therapy alongside DBT, schema therapy, and TFP
It targets loss of mentalising under emotional arousal
Reflective non-skills format suits patients who found DBT mechanical
Repeat trials of a dropped-out modality without addressing dropout are low-yield
The evidence base includes reduced self-harm and improved interpersonal function
explanation.pearls: In context, patients whose core problem is losing the capacity to think about mental states under emotional arousal are the classical MBT indication.

stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 23-year-old woman with a documented diagnosis of borderline personality disorder self-presents at 02:00 having taken 6 paracetamol tablets after a fight with her partner. Her paracetamol level at 4 hours is below the treatment line, LFTs and INR are normal, and she is medically fit for discharge. She is engaged with an established outpatient DBT programme with a dedicated therapist. She has had two similar low-lethality presentations in the past 3 months, both discharged after brief safety planning.

She is now calm, describes the argument as resolved, does not want admission, and is asking to go home to sleep. Her mother is on the way to collect her and she has agreed to attend her regular DBT session in 2 days. There is no acute suicidal intent and no plan disclosed on repeat questioning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/70, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent on air, temperature 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Alert, calm, oriented, reactive affect, no fresh injury, no intoxication.
data_table.Investigations: Serum paracetamol below Rumack-Matthew treatment line at 4 hours. ALT 22, INR 1.0. Ethanol not detected.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition from the emergency department tonight?

options.text: Admit to the acute psychiatric ward for a planned 5-day observation and stabilisation stay
options.rationale: Prolonged admission is not recommended in this disorder as it tends to reinforce maladaptive coping and can disrupt outpatient therapy. Would only be considered when acute risk cannot be managed in the community (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Admit under the state Mental Health Act for involuntary assessment and psychiatric observation
options.rationale: Involuntary detention requires statutory criteria including risk that cannot otherwise be managed; she is engaged, calm, family supported and has an active outpatient plan. Would only be considered if she declined engagement and met the statutory threshold (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Commence low-dose quetiapine 50 mg PRN from the emergency department to manage her future crises
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line and PRN sedation in this population can accumulate harm without addressing the underlying skills gap. Would only be considered short-term in a documented crisis with clear indication (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Refer for a new intake referral to a different DBT programme given her presentations keep occurring
options.rationale: She already has an established DBT therapist and duplicating referrals disrupts continuity and consistency, which are protective. Would only be considered if the existing programme were confirmed to have ended (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

options.text: Discharge home with a written safety plan and early communication with her established DBT therapist
options.rationale: Brief-contact intervention with structured written safety planning, means restriction, family support, and continuity with the existing outpatient therapist is the guideline-recommended approach; inpatient admission is not indicated in the absence of acute risk that cannot be managed in the community (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

explanation.summary: Guideline-based emergency department care of this disorder emphasises brief-contact intervention with written safety planning, means restriction, family support, and continuity with the existing outpatient therapist, avoiding admission where possible.
key_points: Recurrent low-lethality presentations are the norm in this disorder
Prolonged admission tends to reinforce maladaptive coping
Written safety plans, means restriction, and family involvement are core steps
Continuity with the existing outpatient therapist is protective
Involuntary detention is reserved for clearly unmanageable acute risk
explanation.pearls: In context, the guideline default in the emergency department is discharge with structured safety planning and continuity, not admission.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation with a first pregnancy attends your general practice. She has a longstanding diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, is currently 8 months into a DBT programme with good engagement and no self-harm in the last 5 months, and lives with a supportive partner. She has stopped an occasional cannabis habit and does not drink alcohol. Her last two K-10 scores were 18 and 16.

She is asking how to plan for the perinatal period. She reports specific anxiety about how she will manage her emotional reactivity around a newborn, and about whether her own experience of a chaotic childhood will affect her ability to attach to the baby. She is not currently taking psychotropic medication. She has a booked antenatal appointment at the local maternity hospital in 2 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Well, appropriate affect, 20 weeks fundus, foetal heart auscultated.
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods within normal limits at booking. K-10 today 17.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional step to arrange at this visit?

options.text: Commence low-dose sertraline 50 mg daily as prophylaxis against a postpartum decompensation episode
options.rationale: There is no clear indication for antidepressant prophylaxis in the absence of a current depressive episode or a prior severe postpartum illness. Would only be considered for a prior severe episode or current depressive syndrome (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Reduce her DBT contact during pregnancy to avoid overburdening her ahead of the birth event
options.rationale: Continuity of an established therapeutic relationship is protective through the perinatal period and reducing engagement risks decompensation. Would only be considered if the patient herself requested reduction with a specific reason (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

options.text: Refer to a perinatal mental health service for coordinated care including infant mental health input
options.rationale: Guideline-recommended perinatal management for this disorder involves coordinated multidisciplinary planning across obstetrics, mental health, and infant mental health, focused on attachment and parenting support rather than pharmacotherapy in a well-engaged patient (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Advise against breastfeeding preemptively given her personality disorder diagnosis and reactivity
options.rationale: A personality disorder diagnosis is not in itself a contraindication to breastfeeding and pre-emptive advice against it is stigmatising and unsupported. Would only be considered if a specific psychotropic incompatibility applied (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean at 39 weeks to reduce anticipated emotional dysregulation during labour
options.rationale: Mode of birth is decided on obstetric grounds and a personality disorder diagnosis is not itself an indication for elective caesarean. Would only be considered on obstetric grounds (Source: RANZCOG Statement Intrapartum Care).

explanation.summary: Coordinated perinatal mental health care with infant mental health input is the guideline-recommended step for this disorder in pregnancy, focused on attachment support and continuity of an established therapeutic relationship rather than pharmacotherapy in a well-engaged patient.
key_points: Perinatal mental health services coordinate obstetric and mental health care
Infant mental health input focuses on attachment and parenting
Continuity of DBT through pregnancy is protective
Antidepressant prophylaxis is not indicated without prior severe episode or current syndrome
Mode of birth is decided on obstetric grounds
explanation.pearls: In context, the additive step in a well-engaged pregnant patient with this diagnosis is perinatal mental health service linkage, not new medication.

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

stem:
A 16-year-old girl is brought to your child and adolescent mental health clinic by her mother after her fourth episode of superficial cutting in 8 months. Her mother reports 18 months of intense unstable relationships with peers, rapid shifts between idealising and devaluing friends, chronic emptiness, angry outbursts, and difficulty being alone. She has had two low-lethality overdoses in the past year following peer rejections. She has completed a full DSM-5-TR assessment which shows 6 of 9 borderline features present with a persistent pattern for more than 12 months and no active manic or psychotic features.

Her mother has read online that personality disorders should not be diagnosed in adolescence and is asking you to defer any diagnosis until she is 18. She wants to know what evidence-based structured therapy is available if her daughter meets criteria now, and whether waiting would be safer.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, multiple superficial healed and recent linear forearm scars.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 32. FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the mother's question today?

options.text: Defer any personality disorder diagnosis until she turns 18 as the mother has explicitly requested today
options.rationale: Deferral withholds access to evidence-based structured therapy during a critical developmental window and is contrary to current guideline advice. Would only be considered when criteria are clearly not met (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Personality Disorders).

options.text: Explain the diagnosis can be made in adolescence when full criteria are met and refer for adolescent DBT
options.rationale: The RANZCP position and the NHMRC guideline support making the diagnosis in adolescents when full criteria are met with a pattern present for at least 12 months, and early intervention with adolescent DBT reduces self-harm and improves function (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Personality Disorders).

options.text: Commence low-dose fluoxetine 20 mg daily for affective instability while waiting to reassess at age 18 years
options.rationale: SSRIs are not indicated for the core personality disorder and are not a substitute for structured therapy in this age group. Would only be considered for a clearly comorbid depressive episode (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Refer to a general community counselling service for supportive listening without any formal diagnosis attached
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling does not have the evidence base that structured adolescent DBT does for this presentation. Would only be considered if structured therapy were unavailable (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

options.text: Diagnose emerging borderline traits only and avoid the formal disorder label until she becomes a legal adult
options.rationale: When full criteria and duration are met the formal diagnosis is appropriate and using a subthreshold label may block access to guideline-based treatment. Would only be considered when criteria fall short of threshold (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Personality Disorders).

explanation.summary: The RANZCP position statement and the NHMRC guideline support diagnosing borderline personality disorder in adolescents when full criteria and a pattern of at least 12 months are present, and referring for early intervention with adolescent DBT.
key_points: The diagnosis is valid in adolescents when full criteria and 12-month duration are met
Early intervention improves trajectory and reduces self-harm
Adolescent DBT (DBT-A) is the best-evidenced structured therapy in this age group
SSRIs do not treat the core disorder and are not a substitute for therapy
Family involvement is a key component of adolescent programmes
explanation.pearls: In context, deferring the diagnosis until 18 in a case that meets criteria withholds the evidence-based treatment that changes trajectory.

subtopic: Comorbid personality disorder and eating disorder
stem:
A 22-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder and a 4-year history of bulimia nervosa is referred to your community mental health team. She currently has 6 to 8 binge-and-purge episodes per week, weight 58 kg, BMI 20.5, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), and bicarbonate 32 mmol/L (22 to 32). She has recurrent self-harm and two low-lethality overdoses in the past year. She is currently on a DBT waitlist with an expected 3 month wait, and has not yet started any eating disorder specific therapy. She is medically stable today with electrocardiogram showing QTc 440 ms and no U waves.

She is anxious about starting two therapies at once and asks what should be prioritised. She lives alone, has supportive family, and is engaged with her general practitioner. She is not pregnant, is not using illicit substances, and drinks under 2 standard drinks per week.

data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly anxious, weight 58 kg, BMI 20.5, no cardiovascular compromise, no parotid enlargement today.
data_table.Investigations: K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), HCO3 32 mmol/L (22 to 32), Na 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45 to 90), ECG QTc 440 ms, ferritin 45 micrograms/L (30 to 300).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment sequencing plan today?

options.text: Defer all specific therapy until she reaches the top of the DBT waitlist in approximately 3 months
options.rationale: Waiting 3 months while she has symptomatic hypokalaemia and active purging exposes her to avoidable medical risk. Would only be considered if she were medically stable and asymptomatic (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

options.text: Admit for a planned 6 week inpatient stay to address both comorbidities simultaneously as combined care
options.rationale: Prolonged admission is discouraged in the borderline construct and eating disorder guidelines reserve inpatient care for severe medical instability, treatment failure, or high suicide risk. Would only be considered for severe medical instability (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

options.text: Correct hypokalaemia and commence eating disorder focused therapy now while continuing on the DBT waitlist
options.rationale: Bulimia with symptomatic hypokalaemia carries immediate medical risk and requires potassium replacement and eating disorder focused therapy such as CBT-E without delay; personality-focused therapy can proceed in parallel or once the waitlist opens, as the eating disorder is the more urgent life-threatening comorbidity today (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 60 mg daily as sole monotherapy while she remains on the DBT waitlist as planned
options.rationale: Fluoxetine 60 mg is evidence-based for bulimia but is an adjunct rather than a substitute for eating disorder focused therapy and does not address medical instability. Would only be considered as an adjunct to therapy (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

options.text: Prioritise a formal MBT programme first and address the eating disorder afterwards once she is stable
options.rationale: MBT does not directly address bulimic behaviour and delaying eating disorder therapy while she is symptomatically hypokalaemic is medically unsafe. Would only be considered when the eating disorder was in stable remission (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

explanation.summary: When personality disorder coexists with an eating disorder that has current medical instability, guideline-based sequencing addresses the acute medical risk and the eating disorder first while the personality-focused therapy proceeds in parallel or once available.
key_points: Symptomatic hypokalaemia in bulimia is an acute medical concern
CBT-E is first-line for bulimia and can start immediately
Fluoxetine 60 mg is adjunctive in bulimia but is not therapy replacement
Prolonged admission is discouraged in the borderline construct
Personality-focused therapy proceeds in parallel or once the waitlist opens
explanation.pearls: In context, when comorbid conditions coexist, the one causing current medical risk sets the sequencing priority.

subtopic: Personality change due to medical condition
stem:
A 58-year-old previously reserved and conscientious accountant is brought to your clinic by his wife, who reports 14 months of progressive change. He has begun making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, gambled the family savings on impulse, developed a rigid preference for sweet foods and finishes an entire block of chocolate daily, and shows no concern when told his behaviour has cost him his job. He has no history of any personality disorder and premorbid personality was universally described as thoughtful and restrained.

He scores 28 out of 30 on the MMSE and 84 out of 100 on the ACE-III with disproportionate loss on verbal fluency and social cognition subtests, but preserved episodic memory. There is no depression by history, no substance use, no thyroid or B12 deficiency, and no midbrain signs. MRI brain shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

data_table.Examination: Disinhibited in the room, laughs at his wife's tears, mild primitive reflexes present (grasp and palmomental). No focal motor deficit.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits. B12 340 pmol/L. MMSE 28 of 30. ACE-III 84 of 100 with reduced verbal fluency and social cognition subscales. MRI bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis for this presentation?

options.text: New-onset antisocial personality disorder emerging in mid-life following stress
options.rationale: The antisocial construct requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 and is not a valid new-onset diagnosis in mid-life; personality change from a medical or neurological cause must be excluded first. Would only be considered when a lifelong pattern was established (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Late-onset bipolar disorder presenting with hypomanic disinhibition
options.rationale: Late-onset bipolar disorder is uncommon and typically causes episodic distinct mood elevation with reduced sleep need; progressive personality change with executive impairment and structural atrophy is not the picture. Would only be considered with an episodic mood course and no imaging change (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia meeting consensus criteria
options.rationale: Progressive personality change in mid-life with disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive dietary change, impulsivity, executive dysfunction and disproportionately preserved episodic memory alongside frontal and anterior temporal atrophy fulfils the international consensus criteria for behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (Source: Rascovsky international consensus criteria 2011).

options.text: Alzheimer disease presenting atypically with early behavioural symptoms
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease characteristically begins with episodic memory impairment; a leading picture of personality change with preserved memory and frontal atrophy points elsewhere. Would only be considered with an amnestic-first presentation (Source: RANZCP CPG Dementia 2016).

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder producing cognitive and behavioural slowing
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder is characterised by sustained depressed mood and does not produce disinhibition, compulsive dietary change, or frontal atrophy. Would only be considered if the picture were dominated by depressed mood (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Progressive mid-life personality change with disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive eating, impulsivity and executive impairment, with disproportionate frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, fulfils international criteria for behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia.
key_points: New-onset antisocial personality is not a valid mid-life diagnosis
Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia typically presents in the 50s to 60s
Episodic memory is often relatively preserved early
Social cognition and verbal fluency subtests are disproportionately affected
Imaging shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
explanation.pearls: In context, mid-life personality change with preserved memory, executive impairment and frontal atrophy is behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 35-year-old actor is referred by her general practitioner for a personality assessment. Since her early twenties she has been the centre of attention at every social gathering, dresses provocatively, uses dramatic and vague speech, is easily influenced by strong personalities, and considers her professional relationships as far closer than her colleagues do. She feels flat when she is not the focus of attention but does not describe emptiness. She has no history of self-harm, no suicide attempts, no chronic fears of abandonment as a core feature, no rapid shifts between idealising and devaluing individuals, and no impulsive substance use or overdose behaviour.

Her relationships have been shallow but not turbulent; two long-term partners describe her as attention-seeking rather than volatile. She is not currently depressed and is engaged in her acting career. She asks whether her long pattern amounts to a formal diagnosis.

data_table.Examination: Alert, theatrically presented, dramatic gestures, superficial rapport, no thought disorder.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 12. FBC, EUC, LFT within normal limits.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary personality disorder in this presentation?

options.text: Borderline personality disorder with subthreshold self-harm features
options.rationale: The borderline construct requires features including chronic emptiness, recurrent self-harm or suicide behaviour, fears of abandonment, and volatile idealisation-devaluation, which are absent here. Would only be diagnosed when 5 of 9 criteria are met (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Narcissistic personality disorder of the grandiose exhibitionistic subtype
options.rationale: The grandiose narcissistic construct centres on entitlement, exploitation, and inflated self-appraisal; attention-seeking without these core features falls outside it. Would only be diagnosed if grandiosity and exploitation were prominent (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Histrionic personality disorder with sustained attention-seeking presentation
options.rationale: A pervasive pattern from early adulthood of excessive attention-seeking, dramatic and vague speech, provocative appearance, suggestibility, and considering relationships as more intimate than they are, without the self-harm, abandonment fears, and volatile idealisation-devaluation of the borderline construct, characterises this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder with associated interpersonal emptiness features
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires sustained depressed mood for at least 2 years with vegetative features, which are not described. Would only be diagnosed with sustained low mood (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Bipolar II disorder with recurrent past hypomanic episodes and current euthymia
options.rationale: Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic episodes of at least 4 days with a change in functioning; enduring attention-seeking without episodic mood elevation does not meet criteria. Would only be diagnosed with a discrete hypomanic episode (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: The histrionic construct is a declining diagnosis but remains in DSM-5-TR. Its features are excessive attention-seeking, dramatic and vague speech, suggestibility and perceived closeness in shallow relationships, without the volatility and self-harm of the borderline construct.
key_points: Histrionic diagnosis persists in DSM-5-TR though its use is declining
Attention-seeking without self-harm, abandonment fear or volatile idealisation is the discriminator from the borderline construct
Overlap with the borderline construct exists but the two are distinguishable on core features
The grandiose narcissistic construct requires entitlement and exploitation
Comorbidity with mood disorders is common and can mask the personality picture
explanation.pearls: In context, attention-seeking dramaticism without self-harm and without volatile idealisation-devaluation points to the histrionic rather than the borderline construct.

stem:
A 42-year-old accountant is referred by his general practitioner after his wife complained he is impossible to live with. He describes a lifelong preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism that interferes with completing tax returns because they are never quite good enough, excessive devotion to work at the expense of leisure and family, rigid morality, hoarding of worn-out items, reluctance to delegate at work because others cannot meet his standards, miserliness, and stubbornness. He experiences these traits as consistent with his values and does not want to change them.

He does not have unwanted intrusive thoughts that he tries to resist, and does not perform time-consuming rituals to neutralise anxiety. He is not depressed and does not use substances.

data_table.Examination: Alert, meticulously dressed, precise speech, no obvious rituals in the room.

lead_in: Which is the most likely primary diagnosis in this presentation?

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder with contamination-related intrusive obsessions
options.rationale: The disorder requires ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions and compulsive behaviours performed to reduce anxiety, which he does not describe. Would only be diagnosed with obsessions and compulsions (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder with prominent perfectionistic worry across domains
options.rationale: Generalised anxiety requires excessive worry across multiple domains for at least 6 months with physical anxiety symptoms; enduring perfectionism without worry does not meet criteria. Would only be diagnosed with pervasive worry (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder with lifelong ego-syntonic perfectionism
options.rationale: A lifelong ego-syntonic pattern of preoccupation with order, perfectionism impairing task completion, workaholism, rigidity, miserliness and stubbornness, without unwanted intrusive obsessions or compulsions performed to neutralise anxiety, characterises this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder recognised for the first time in adulthood
options.rationale: Autism spectrum diagnosis requires early-childhood social communication difference and restricted repetitive behaviours; work-related perfectionism alone does not meet the framework. Would only be diagnosed with early social communication difference and restricted interests (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Hoarding disorder with prominent clutter compromising his living space at home
options.rationale: Hoarding disorder requires persistent difficulty discarding due to a perceived need to save and resulting clutter compromising living space; his hoarding is a single trait within a broader personality picture. Would only be diagnosed when hoarding dominates (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: OCPD is an ego-syntonic personality pattern characterised by perfectionism, orderliness, workaholism and rigidity, without the intrusive obsessions and neutralising compulsions of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
key_points: OCPD is ego-syntonic and lifelong
OCD is ego-dystonic with intrusive thoughts and neutralising compulsions
Miserliness and hoarding of worn-out items are OCPD features
Generalised anxiety requires pervasive worry across domains
Comorbidity between OCPD and OCD is possible but not the same diagnosis
explanation.pearls: In context, ego-syntonic lifelong perfectionism without intrusive obsessions and rituals is the OCPD construct rather than obsessive-compulsive disorder.
